deep.reconstruction:
The page has no formulas. It is the title and introduction of a fair-copy draft of what became Riemann's 1860 memoir 'Ueber die Fortpflanzung ebener Luftwellen von endlicher Schwingungsweite' (Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 8; author's announcement in Göttinger Nachrichten 1859). The draft title here is 'Zur Aerodynamik'. The content is programmatic.

(1) Setting. The Euler equations of compressible gas motion have long been known. They have been integrated almost only when the pressure differences are infinitesimal fractions of the total pressure, i.e. by linearised acoustics, keeping first-order terms. Only recently did Helmholtz (1856, combination tones) keep second-order terms, explaining the objective origin of combination tones.

(2) Claim. Suppose the initial motion is everywhere in one direction, and velocity u and pressure p are constant on each plane perpendicular to it. This is plane, one-dimensional flow u(x,t), p(x,t), rho(x,t). Then the exact nonlinear equations can be integrated completely:
- rho_t + (rho u)_x = 0
- u_t + u u_x + p_x/rho = 0

In the memoir this is done with the Riemann invariants r, s = u ± ∫ sqrt(φ'(ρ)) dρ/ρ and the hodograph/Riemann-function method. None of that appears on this page.

(3) Motivation. For acoustics the linear theory suffices. The exact results might give 'Anhaltspunkte' to meteorology, and nonlinear PDEs are of theoretical interest.

(4) Equation of state. If temperature differences equalised instantly, Mariotte's (Boyle's) law p = C ρ would apply. Riemann argues instead that heat exchange is negligible. One must therefore use the adiabatic law, i.e. the law for a gas that neither takes up nor gives off heat. The next page derives it as p = C ρ^k with k = c_p/c_v (Poisson).

Implicit consequence (mine): the isothermal sound speed is sqrt(p/ρ) (Newton) and the adiabatic one is sqrt(k p/ρ) (Laplace).
errors: No mathematical errors on the page. The physical assertion that heat exchange is negligible is the standard Laplace/Poisson adiabatic assumption and is correct for sound waves.

The completeness claim ('vollständig integriren') is somewhat optimistic. In the memoir the solution is complete only up to the formation of discontinuities (shocks). At shocks Riemann's own jump treatment conserved entropy rather than energy, an error later corrected (Rankine 1870, Hugoniot 1887, Rayleigh 1910). None of this is on this page.

results.what: Programme: exact integration of the 1D isentropic Euler equations for plane waves of finite amplitude, in contrast to first-order (and Helmholtz second-order) acoustics
results.modern_name: Riemann problem / Riemann invariants / method of characteristics for 1D gas dynamics (nonlinear acoustics, simple waves)
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann 1860 (with Earnshaw 1858/1860 and Poisson 1808 for simple waves)

results.what: Choice of adiabatic (Poisson) rather than isothermal (Mariotte/Boyle) pressure–density law
results.modern_name: Isentropic equation of state p = C*rho^gamma (Laplace correction to the sound speed)

results.what: Reference to Helmholtz's second-order treatment explaining objective combination tones

deep.surprise_reason: This is the introduction of Riemann's well-known 1860 shock-wave paper, almost verbatim with the published text. The only novelty is the draft title 'Zur Aerodynamik' and minor manuscript edits. There is no mathematics beyond what is published.

checkable.asserts: For the adiabatic law p=A*rho^k, dp/drho = k p/rho (squared adiabatic sound speed); result 0
For Mariotte/Boyle p=A*rho, dp/drho = p/rho (Newton's isothermal sound speed squared); result 0
